newsitem.title: USA: Cuyahoga treasurer "delighted" with ruling - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Cuyahoga treasurer "delighted" with ruling - lawyer.

text.p: Retired Cuyahoga County Treasurer Francis Gaul was "delighted" with an appeals court ruling that cleared him of a misdemeanor charge related to a failed county investment fund, Gaul's lawyer said Tuesday.
The Ohio Court of Appeals Friday overturned Gaul's 1995 conviction for dereliction of duty and issued an acquittal.
"Mr. Gaul is delighted," lawyer Mark DeVan said in a telephone interview. "He feels the justice system vindicated him, and his long nightmare is now over."
County prosecutors did not immediately return phone calls.

In 1994, amid rising interest rates and a declining bond market, county commissioners shut down the treasurer's Secured Assets Fund Earnings (SAFE) fund after they learned of paper losses, risky investment strategies and leveraging.
Shutting down the $1 billion-plus fund cost the county $114 million. None of the other 70-plus local governments that invested in it lost money.

Gaul, 70, was convicted in 1995. The misdemeanor conviction could have meant 90 days in jail and a $750 fine. But the Ohio Court of Appeals panel of three judges from outside Cuyahoga County said prosecutors did not demonstrate Gaul committed a crime.

"We do not suggest that Gaul is blameless in failing to supervise improvident investment activities of his subordinates," the panel wrote. But he should not have been found guilty on the misdemeanor charge, the panel said.

It added that in Ohio, public officials may be personally liable for lost public monies, and, "should civil litigation follow this appeal... we cannot determine from the record whether all of Gaul's actions complied with the requirements" of Ohio law that would protect him from liablity.
Gaul, county treasurer since 1975, retired March 1, six months before his term was due to expire.

Another official, Timothy Simmerly, former chief of the treasurer's investment department, was sentenced to three years' probation and fined $1,750 after pleading guilty to dereliction of duty and falsification, also a misdemeanor.
In addition, a state and county lawsuit is pending, which accuses six brokerages and a bank of negligence and violating fiduciary duty. It seeks unspecified damages.
